title: Using qualitative approaches to improve quantitative inferences in environmental psychology
author: Lewis, Bravo, et al.

steps.title: Form partnership and recruit participants
steps.instruction: Partner with the Environmental Defense Fund to access Latina/o community organizations in San Antonio, Texas (ZIP 78207). Recruit 24 representatives from 16 distinct Hispanic/Latino community organizations (e.g., voter registration, business development, culture and arts, healthy‑food access).

steps.title: Schedule focus‑group sessions
steps.instruction: Arrange three semi‑structured focus‑group discussions at a community‑center in a low‑income Westside neighborhood. Each group should contain 6–9 participants plus one moderator and three additional research‑team observers (who take notes but do not sit at the main table). Plan for each session to last about 1.5 hours.

steps.title: Obtain consent and set expectations
steps.instruction: Upon arrival, have each participant read and sign an informed‑consent form. Explain that the discussion aims to learn about “issues facing your community in San Antonio,” that there are no right or wrong answers, and that the goal is to generate a broad list of issue priorities rather than reach consensus.

steps.title: Conduct semi‑structured interview
steps.instruction: Follow the adapted Krueger & Casey protocol:

substeps.instruction: a. Ask participants to privately reflect for ~1 minute, then invite each person to state three issues they consider most important to the Latina/o community in San Antonio; record each issue on a large notepad visible to all.

b. After all have spoken, prompt participants to generate the most important environmental issues facing their communities, again allowing a brief pause for reflection; add novel issues to the same notepad.
c. Ask participants to name any issues not yet mentioned.
d. Pose the closing question: “If you could tell the mayor of San Antonio one thing, what would it be?” Record responses.
e. Throughout, the moderator remains mainly passive, intervening only to request clarification or to relate new issues to those already listed.

steps.title: Record data and debrief participants
steps.instruction: Audio‑record one of the three focus groups for transcription (the others rely on handwritten notes). Have the notetaker write all issues on the large sheet. At the end, thank participants, give each a paper survey for additional comments, and provide a debriefing form with contact information.

steps.title: Transcribe notes and upload securely
steps.instruction: After leaving the venue, the on‑site senior research team transcribes handwritten notes and uploads the typed versions to a secure server. Return to campus for further processing.

steps.title: Digitize notepad and audio files
steps.instruction: Graduate‑student team members transcribe the large‑notepad posters from each focus group into digital files. Transcribe the audio file from the recorded group (but do not use it for coding to avoid data imbalance).

steps.title: Code and analyze issue data
steps.instruction: Perform a frequency count of issue mentions per group (Group 1: 34 issues; Group 2: 22 issues; Group 3: 16 issues). Identify convergence across groups by noting issues that appear in all three. Discuss identified common themes with the larger research team to inform subsequent survey development.
